world_behind.title: The end of a long argument
world_behind.text: Six chapters have run from the crisis under Ahaz through the Assyrian rod to the shoot out of Jesse's stump. This is where that sequence lands. It is the only chapter in the block made entirely of praise, and it is the shortest one Nephi copied.

world_behind.title: Two songs, one singular and one plural
world_behind.text: Verse 1 begins "thou shalt say" and verse 4 begins "shall ye say." The first is one person's thanksgiving and the second is a congregation's. Isaiah gives the same day two liturgies, which is how a community usually receives good news: privately first, then out loud together.

world_behind.title: Verbs for a public square
world_behind.text: Praise, call, declare, make mention, sing, cry out, shout. Nothing in the chapter is done quietly and nothing is done alone after verse 3. The instruction is not to feel grateful but to make noise where other people can hear it.

world_behind.title: Zion addressed as one person
world_behind.text: Verse 6 speaks to "thou inhabitant of Zion" in the singular, as though the whole city were a single resident. The block has used that figure for judgment already, with Jerusalem sitting on the ground. Here the same single figure is told to shout.

world_behind.title: Water you have to go get
world_behind.text: Wells in a dry country are not springs; someone walks to them with a jar and hauls. Verse 3 puts joy on the action rather than on the arrival, which for a colony that had crossed a desert and an ocean to reach a promised land would not have read as decoration.

world_behind.title: Almost exact, again
world_behind.text: As with the chapter before it, the differences from the King James text amount to one word. Two chapters running, the record's Isaiah and the Bible's Isaiah are effectively the same text, which is a fact worth holding beside the chapters where they are not.

words.text: An old second-person past form: you comforted me. The awkwardness of the ending is worth keeping, because it puts the whole clause in the mouth of someone speaking directly to God rather than about him. The verse's three verbs are all addressed the same way, praise, wast angry, comfortedst, and the middle one is not softened.

In older usage, surpassing, higher than the rest, closer to exalted than to very good. It describes what the Lord has done rather than how well he did it. The next clause says the result is known in all the earth, so the word is measuring reach as much as quality.

phrases.text: The block has ended four sections with the opposite sentence: his anger is not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. It tolls in the vineyard chapter, three times in chapter 19, and once more in chapter 20. Here, in the first line of the praise chapter, the refrain is finally reversed. Nephi copied every stroke of the bell and then this, and the arrangement does the work without a word of commentary.

phrases.term: the Lord Jehovah is my strength and my song
phrases.text: The line comes from Israel's oldest song, sung at the sea after the escape from Egypt: "The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation" (Ex. 15:2). Isaiah hands a rescued people the words their ancestors used, and the record's one substantive difference here is a tense, "he also has become my salvation" (v. 2), a thing completed rather than occurring. The divine name is also left standing rather than replaced by a title, and it appears only twice in the whole record, here and on Moroni's last page, so a reader meets it in this verse and then not again for a thousand years of narrative.

spans.text: he also has become my salvation

phrases.term: draw water out of the wells of salvation
phrases.text: The chapter's one image, and it is a chore. Drawing water was daily, female, and heavy work in that world, and a well is a dug shaft rather than a spring, requiring a rope, a jar, and a walk. The verse attaches joy to the drawing rather than to the drinking, and the plural is not accidental: salvation is pictured as a source people go back to, which is a different promise from a fountain that comes to you.

phrases.term: declare his doings among the people
phrases.text: The psalm gives nearly the same instruction in nearly the same order, "call upon his name: make known his deeds among the people" (Ps. 105:1). Both put declaring to others immediately after calling on God, with nothing in between. Praise in this tradition is not finished until somebody outside the room has heard about it.

phrases.term: this is known in all the earth
phrases.text: The scope claim, and it is stated as a fact rather than a hope. What began as one person's thanksgiving in verse 1 has become, four verses later, common knowledge on the whole planet. The chapter's movement is entirely outward: private, congregational, then universal, in six verses.

phrases.term: great is the Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee
phrases.text: The title Jacob used thirteen times in one sermon closes the block's first movement, and the preposition is the point: in the midst. Zephaniah promises the same presence in almost the same words, "the king of Israel, even the LORD, is in the midst of thee" (Zeph. 3:15). After six chapters in which God has been a rod, a fire, and a hidden face, the last word about him is proximity.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: Praise that keeps the anger in it
verses.text: The thanksgiving does not pretend the anger never happened. It says thou wast angry, then says the anger is turned away, then says thou comfortedst me, in that order. A song that skipped the first clause would be a different and lesser song, and the block has spent five chapters earning the middle one.

verses.label: v. 2
verses.title: Trust stated twice, in old words
verses.text: "I will trust, and not be afraid" (v. 2) is the decision; the rest of the verse is the reason, and the reason is quoted from the song at the Red Sea. The speaker is not producing a new confidence. He is reaching for the sentence his people already had and finding that it still fits.

cites.quote: I will trust, and not be afraid

spans.text: I will trust, and not be afraid

verses.label: v. 3
verses.title: The one picture
verses.text: Everything else in the chapter is verbs of speech. This verse alone gives an image, and it is domestic: a walk to the well, a rope, a jar, and joy in the doing. Whatever enormous events the block has described, the chapter's single illustration of salvation is a household errand.

verses.label: v. 4
verses.title: Four things to do with the news
verses.text: Praise, call, declare, make mention. Two are directed at God and two at other people, and they alternate. Verse 4 is the practical instruction of the chapter, and it assumes an audience: his doings go among the people, and his name is made much of in public.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: Singing, and what the song accomplishes
verses.text: The command is to sing, the reason is that he has done surpassing things, and the result is that this is known everywhere. The verse quietly claims that the singing is part of how the knowing happens. Nothing else in the chapter is offered as the mechanism.

verses.label: v. 6
verses.title: Shout, because he is near
verses.text: The last verse gives the loudest instruction and the smallest reason. Cry out and shout, not because of a victory or a rescue described, but because the Holy One of Israel is in the middle of the city. The block that opened with a mountain far above the hills ends its first movement with God standing in the neighborhood.

chapter.title: The refrain is finally answered
chapter.text: Four times the block has closed a movement with anger not turned away and a hand still stretched out. Verse 1 says the anger is turned away. Nothing in the chapter announces that it is answering anything, and a reader who has been through chapters 15 to 20 in order does not need to be told.

chapter.title: Praise is the block's rarest register
chapter.text: Of thirteen chapters Nephi copied, this is the only one with no judgment in it at all. Its brevity is part of its function: six verses of thanksgiving against six chapters of warning is roughly the ratio Isaiah works in, and the record preserves the proportion rather than rebalancing it.

chapter.title: The chapter moves outward in six steps
chapter.text: One voice, then a congregation, then the peoples, then all the earth. Each verse widens the audience without changing the content, which is a structure a reader can feel before noticing. The last verse then reverses the motion and puts God in the middle of the city.

chapter.title: Old words for a new rescue
chapter.text: The song at the sea, the psalm's instruction, Zephaniah's promise: this chapter is largely made of sentences Israel already had. Isaiah's contribution is the occasion rather than the wording, which is itself a claim about how deliverance works. It repeats.

chapter.title: Two chapters running with no variants
chapter.text: Chapters 21 and 22 are effectively identical to the King James text. The block's readings diverge in some places and not others, and this pair is the clearest evidence that whatever produces the differences is not operating uniformly.

chapter.title: A colony's own song
chapter.text: Nephi's people had been brought out of a doomed city, across a desert, and over an ocean. A chapter that hands the exodus song to the next generation of rescued people is about as directly likenable as the block gets, and he copied it without adding a line.

applications.title: Keep the anger in the sentence
applications.text: When you thank God for something resolved, say the hard middle out loud too: this was painful, and it has passed. Gratitude that edits out the difficulty tends not to survive the next one.

applications.title: Borrow somebody else’s words
applications.text: Find a line from scripture, a hymn, or your own family's history that fit somebody else's rescue, and use it about yours this week, in their words rather than new ones. Isaiah's speaker did exactly that.

applications.title: Go get the water
applications.text: Salvation in this chapter is drawn, not delivered. Name the specific thing you have been waiting to receive passively, and do the walking part of it once, on a set day, with the jar.

applications.title: Declare one doing
applications.text: Tell one person this week something specific God has done for you, without generalizing it into a principle. The verse pairs calling on his name with saying it out loud among people, and it does not treat the second as optional.

applications.title: Notice the middle
applications.text: The reason for shouting is proximity, not outcome. Before asking for a change in your circumstances, spend one prayer entirely on the fact that he is in the midst, and see whether the request changes shape.

questions.text: What am I still angry about that I would have to name before I could honestly say it had passed?
Whose rescue am I willing to borrow words from, and does that make my own smaller or larger?
What have I been treating as a fountain that God seems to be offering as a well?
When did I last declare a specific doing rather than a general belief?
If singing is part of how a thing becomes known, what am I keeping quiet that should be sung?
Do I believe he is in the midst of my situation, and what would change today if I did?
